analysis.one_liner: Repeals oil and gas tax breaks and redirects the money to low-income heating aid and home weatherization.
analysis.headline: The bill would have repealed oil and gas tax subsidies to fund $15 billion in heating assistance and $7.38 billion in weatherization, but it died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out a set of federal tax breaks for the oil and gas industry — some newly created by the Energy Policy Act of 2005 and some decades old — including credits for enhanced oil recovery, low-sulfur diesel, and unconventional fuels, plus a long-standing deduction for drilling costs. It would then spend $15 billion on emergency home-heating aid for low-income households (LIHEAP) and $7.38 billion on weatherizing homes to cut energy bills. It was referred to four committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households struggling with home heating bills would gain, through $15 billion in emergency LIHEAP funds and $7.38 billion for the Energy Department's weatherization program, which insulates and repairs homes to permanently lower energy costs [S2][S3]. Taxpayers generally would gain from ending subsidies to a highly profitable industry. Weatherization contractors would gain work under the expanded program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households facing high heating bills

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates $15 billion for emergency low-income home energy assistance through HHS, available through 2015, to help poor households pay heating and cooling bills.
Appropriates $7.38 billion to the Department of Energy for weatherization assistance, which pays to insulate and repair low-income homes so their energy bills drop permanently.

Pays for the aid by repealing oil and gas tax breaks, including the new 2005 provisions allowing refiners to immediately expense 50% of refinery property costs and faster write-offs of exploration costs, plus older credits for enhanced oil recovery, low-sulfur diesel, and nonconventional fuels, and the deduction for intangible drilling costs — shifting the cost of energy policy away from taxpayers and onto the industry.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and refiners, who would lose the enhanced oil recovery credit, low-sulfur diesel credit, nonconventional fuel credit, refinery expensing, geological and geophysical amortization, the sulfur-compliance deduction, and the intangible drilling cost deduction. To the extent the industry keeps prices up rather than absorbing the cost, some of it could be passed to consumers at the pump.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and refiners

drawbacks.text: Repealing the drilling, refining, and fuel-production tax breaks could raise the cost of domestic oil and gas production, and energy companies would likely pass some of that through to consumers in the form of higher fuel prices.

The bill appropriates $22.38 billion in new spending (designated as 'emergency' under the budget resolution) while the revenue from repealing the subsidies may not fully match it in the first year, adding to the deficit in the near term.
With only one cosponsor, the bill had no realistic path forward, and its all-or-nothing approach (repeal everything, fund everything) gave members who might support pieces of it no middle option.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill made an even trade on its face: end taxpayer subsidies to a highly profitable industry and use the money to help low-income families heat and weatherize their homes. The real costs are the risk of somewhat higher fuel prices if producers pass the tax change through, and the possibility that first-year revenue falls short of the $22.38 billion in appropriations. Those costs are modest and speculative; the benefits are direct and targeted at people who literally face choosing between heating and other necessities. The main flaw is design, not substance: the bill was written as a maximalist statement with essentially no cosponsor support, which is part of why it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee — sent to four of them and then parked in subcommittees — and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders, an independent, and Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on November 18, 2005, a few months after the Energy Policy Act of 2005 had added new tax breaks for oil and gas.

The Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Budget — a multi-committee referral that makes progress harder because each committee must act on its piece.
In December 2005 and March 2006 the bill was referred to subcommittees (Energy and Air Quality, and Education Reform), which is where legislation typically goes to wait.
No further action was ever taken, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and refiners, who kept every one of the tax subsidies the bill would have repealed. Low-income households never received the additional heating and weatherization money it would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies kept their subsidies

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal oil and gas tax subsidies and fund LIHEAP and weatherization.

for.name: Dennis Kucinich
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill; the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Republican majority, 109th Congress
against.role: Majority party controlling the committees and floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or a floor vote; it was referred to subcommittees in December 2005 and March 2006 and never acted on again.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the sponsor was an independent, its single cosponsor a Democrat, and the Republican-controlled committees never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the enhanced oil recovery credit, the nonconventional fuel credit, the deduction for intangible drilling costs, and amortization of exploration costs — long-standing features of the tax code that reduce what producers owe. The industry kept all of them when the bill died in committee.

It would repeal the 2005 provision letting refiners immediately expense 50% of refinery property costs and the deduction for capital costs of complying with sulfur regulations — a targeted new subsidy the industry had just won and would have lost.

The low-sulfur diesel credit and the nonconventional fuel production credit would end, raising costs for cleaner diesel and alternative fuels; whether that helps or hurts the public depends on whether one views those credits as useful clean-energy policy or wasteful subsidy.
A $7.38 billion expansion of the Energy Department weatherization program would have generated years of paid work insulating and repairing low-income homes.
